title: Despair not
hook: despair not of God's mercy, for God forgives all sins (Quran 39:53)
carry: even if your sins reached the clouds

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nickel Mines, and neighbors at a grieving door. Your line was the other family. Who did you give a thought to? Today, the Christian voices give way to Muslim voices, starting with a verse of the Qur'an. Day nine hundred fifty-six.

Two in the morning, and somebody is awake, replaying something they did years ago. A word said in anger. A friend let down. A thing nobody else knows about. It has been forgiven by others, maybe, or forgotten by them. But not by the one lying awake. There's a voice in that kind of night that says: too late, too much, this one stays. The Qur'an has a verse spoken straight into that voice. It doesn't start with a rule. It starts by naming the people it's talking to. Today: al-Ghafur.
screen: `AWAKE AT TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `TOO LATE, TOO MUCH.` → `A VERSE SPOKEN INTO THAT VOICE.`

segments.voice: First, who it's for. The verse opens with a command to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to speak in God's name. In Pickthall's translation: "Say: O My slaves who have been prodigal to their own hurt!" Prodigal, here, means people who have gone too far, wasting themselves, hurting their own souls. Notice the word My. Not those people: My slaves, belonging to God. The ones who went too far are still addressed as His. Second, the command. "Despair not of the mercy of Allah." Notice what's being forbidden. Not the wrong, at least not in this line. Despair. The verse treats hopelessness about mercy as its own kind of mistake, as if to say the door is not the problem; believing it's locked is. Third, the reach. The verse continues: "Who forgiveth all sins." All. The next verse calls people to turn to their Lord and surrender to Him before a reckoning comes, and the promise is read together with that turning back. Read that way, the mercy isn't a reason to stop caring. It's a reason not to give up. Fourth, the name. The verse ends: "Lo! He is the Forgiving, the Merciful." The Forgiving, in Arabic, is al-Ghafur, one of the names Muslims use for God. There's a saying of the Prophet, recorded by at-Tirmidhi, that puts it vividly: in it God says that even if a person's sins reached the clouds of the sky, and they asked forgiveness, God would forgive them. For Muslims who pray with this verse, it answers the late-night voice that says too late with two words: despair not.
screen: `O MY SLAVES: STILL CALLED MINE.` · `DESPAIR IS WHAT'S FORBIDDEN.` · `ALL SINS, AND A TURNING BACK.` · `THE FORGIVING, THE MERCIFUL.` · then, large: `DESPAIR NOT OF THE MERCY OF ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop, and breathe out a little longer than you breathe in. Let one old guilt you still carry come up. Something already done and over, that you've said sorry for or can't fix now. Hold it the way the verse holds the people it speaks to: as someone who went too far, and is still called by name. Notice the voice that says it's too late. Don't argue with it. Just set the verse's two words beside it: despair not. Breathe out, and let the weight loosen a little, even if it doesn't leave. If you pray, you can ask forgiveness in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Al-Ghafur. The Forgiving, a name for God in Islam, from the verse that tells those who went too far: despair not. Today's word.
Your line: even if your sins reached the clouds. Today, when an old guilt comes back, answer it with that line, and let one thing go that you've already made right. Day nine hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims seek God's forgiveness, called istighfar, in prayer and in their own words, and call on God by names such as al-Ghafur, the Forgiving.

fork.setup: the verse speaks to people who have gone too far and hurt their own souls. what's the first thing it tells them not to do?
options: not to pray until they've made amends.
not to despair of God's mercy.
not to speak of what they did.
fork.reveal: "despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins." the thing forbidden here is hopelessness.

original.note: Arabic: the Forgiving, as Qur'an 39:53 names God.

trapdoor: what you thought: a verse saying anything goes.
what it means: a word to those who went too far: you are still called Mine, and despair is the mistake.
what a scholar hears: the verse opens with Say, a command to the Prophet, and is read together with the next verse's call to turn back.

notes: Muslim voices begin here (days 956 on). The review notes the shift from the Christian voices.

Pickthall 1930 wording of 39:53 should be checked word for word ('Say: O My slaves who have been prodigal to their own hurt! Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins. Lo! He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.').
Hadith qudsi on sins reaching the clouds of the sky (anan as-sama'), paraphrased: confirm the number Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3540 and the wording.
'Prodigal, here, means people who have gone too far, wasting themselves' is a gloss on Pickthall's English, not an Arabic etymology; confirm.
Muslim scholars also teach that wrongs against other people require making amends with them; the voice doesn't raise it, as tomorrow and later Muslim days may. A Keeper may want a line on it.
'Al-Ghafur, one of the names Muslims use for God' makes no count of the names on purpose.
Original: ٱلْغَفُور with wasla and vowels; confirm spelling and pronunciation.

Editor pass: 'God's first word to them is My ... My servants' corrected (the verse opens with Say, and Pickthall has slaves); 'Muslim teachers read' made passive per the claims rule; 'before the time runs out' made 'before a reckoning comes' (39:54); stock 'for anyone' close and practice opener varied.

Audit (2026-10-01): closing line rewritten: it was garbled ('whoever hears it') and leaned toward telling the listener their despair is wrong; now describes how Muslims use the verse. 'Mercy isn't a reason to stop caring' attributed to the reading ('Read that way'); 'Not you people' made 'Not those people'.
